title: The dumb ox
hookLine: Thomas Aquinas is so quiet classmates mock him; his teacher says this ox's bellow will fill the world

lines: THEY CALL HIM THE DUMB OX.
cards: In the classroom there's a young friar who hardly ever speaks. He's big, slow-moving, from a noble Italian family, and he sits through every lecture and every argument in silence, taking it in.
His classmates have a name for him: the dumb ox. In their Latin, dumb meant mute, not stupid, but the joke cut both ways: a large animal that doesn't make a sound.
One of them, feeling sorry for him, offers to help him with his lessons. The quiet friar says thank you, and lets him. His name is Thomas Aquinas.

teach.b: William of Tocco, who wrote an early life of Thomas, tells what happened next. The kind classmate began explaining a lesson, got lost halfway, and couldn't find his way out.
Thomas gently picked up the thread and explained it clearly, and the classmate asked him to be the tutor from then on.
The master of that school was Albert, a Dominican scholar later called Albert the Great. He noticed the quiet one and set him a hard question to argue in front of everyone.
Thomas answered it so well that Albert turned to the room. The account gives his words like this: you call him the dumb ox, but one day his bellowing will be heard throughout the world.
Thomas went on to teach at Paris and wrote the Summa Theologiae, laying out questions about God and the world in yesterday's disputation pattern: question, objections, answer, reply.

teach.h: THE SUMMA, AND A DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.
teach.b: Catholics count him a Doctor of the Church, and his writing is still read in seminaries and universities. The ox did bellow.
But the silence came first. Tradition remembers Thomas, even after he was known, as gentle in argument, slow to speak and careful with other people's views.

teach.h: A TIME TO KEEP SILENCE, AND A TIME TO SPEAK.
teach.b: The Douay-Rheims Ecclesiastes says there is "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak." For Thomas, the first time made the second one possible. The room underrated him because he wasn't loud.
His teacher heard what the room missed.

how: Catholics honor Thomas Aquinas as a saint and Doctor of the Church; his feast is kept in the Church's calendar, and his Summa Theologiae is studied in seminaries and Catholic universities.

o: the classmates' nickname for silent Thomas
an insult for a student who failed exams
a farm animal that pulled the monks' plow

games.q: the dumb ox — tap the pairs.
p: Thomas's teacher, who set the hard question
offered to tutor Thomas, then got lost
wrote an early life of Thomas

s: the nickname meant his classmates thought he couldn't think
dumb meant mute: they mocked his silence, and some took it for slowness. his teacher saw otherwise.
Thomas turned down the classmate's offer of help
he accepted it gratefully, and ended up explaining the lesson himself.
Albert said the ox's bellowing would be heard throughout the world
so the account in William of Tocco tells it.

games.q: you're Thomas. a well-meaning classmate offers to tutor you in something you already understand. what do you do?
o: tell him politely that you already know it.
thank him and let him teach you.
show him up in front of the class.
games.why: Thomas accepted. when the classmate got lost, Thomas quietly helped him through, and the classmate asked him to be the tutor.

practice: Think of one quiet person: a colleague who rarely speaks up, a relative at the end of the table, a child who watches more than talks. Hold them in mind kindly, and wonder what they've noticed that the loud people missed.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, simply wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Dumb ox. The nickname classmates gave the silent young Thomas Aquinas, until his teacher Albert said his bellowing would be heard throughout the world. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a mute ox, the classmates' joke about the silent Thomas.
